title: About Norovirus

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Norovirus is a very contagious virus that causes vomiting and diarrhea.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: It is sometimes called the "stomach flu" or the "stomach bug." However, norovirus illness is not related to the flu. The flu is caused by the influenza virus. Norovirus causes acute gastroenteritis, an inflammation of the stomach or intestines.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Most people with norovirus illness get better within 1 to 3 days; but they can still spread the virus for a few days after.

sections.heading: Types
sections.text: You can get norovirus illness many times in your life because there are many different types of noroviruses. Infection with one type of norovirus may not protect you against other types.

sections.heading: Types
sections.text: It is possible to develop protection against specific types. But it is not known exactly how long protection lasts. This may explain why so many people of all ages get infected during norovirus outbreaks.

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: A person usually develops symptoms 12 to 48 hours after being exposed to norovirus.

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Most common symptoms: Diarrhea, vomiting, nausea, stomach pain

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Other symptoms: Fever, headache, and body aches

sections.heading: Dehydration
sections.text: If you have norovirus illness, you can feel extremely ill, and vomit or have diarrhea many times a day. This can lead to dehydration (loss of body fluids), especially in young children, older adults, and people with other illnesses. Symptoms of dehydration include:

sections.heading: Dehydration
sections.text: Decreased urination

sections.heading: Dehydration
sections.text: Dry mouth and throat

sections.heading: Dehydration
sections.text: Feeling dizzy when standing up

sections.heading: Dehydration
sections.text: Crying with few or no tears

sections.heading: Dehydration
sections.text: Unusual sleepiness or fussiness

sections.heading: Who is at risk
sections.text: Anyone can get infected and sick with norovirus and people of all ages get infected during norovirus outbreaks. Your likelihood of getting a norovirus infection is also determined in part by your genes.

sections.heading: Who is at risk
sections.text: If eaten raw, oysters and other filter-feeding shellfish can contain viruses and bacteria that can cause illness or death. Anyone who consumes raw shellfish is at risk of contracting norovirus. Children younger than 5 years old, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems are more likely to develop severe infections.

sections.heading: How it spreads
sections.text: Norovirus spreads very easily and quickly in different ways. You can get norovirus by:

sections.heading: How it spreads
sections.text: Having direct contact with someone with norovirus, like caring for them, sharing food or eating utensils with them, or eating food handled by them.

sections.heading: How it spreads
sections.text: Eating food or drinking liquids that are contaminated with norovirus.

sections.heading: How it spreads
sections.text: Touching contaminated objects or surfaces and then putting your unwashed fingers in your mouth.

sections.heading: How it spreads
sections.text: You can still spread norovirus for 2 weeks or more after you feel better.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Norovirus is very contagious, but you can take steps to protect yourself and others, including:

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Wash your hands well and often.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Cook shellfish thoroughly and wash fruits and vegetables.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Clean and disinfect contaminated surfaces.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Wash laundry in hot water.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Stay home when sick for 2 days (48 hours) after symptoms stop.

sections.heading: Testing and diagnosis
sections.text: Diagnostic methods for norovirus focus on detecting viral RNA (genetic material) or viral antigen. Diagnostic tests are available at all public health laboratories and many clinical laboratories.

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
sections.text: Most people with norovirus illness get better within 1 to 3 days. There is no specific medicine to treat people with norovirus illness. Antibiotic drugs will not help treat norovirus infections because they fight bacteria, not viruses.

sections.heading: Watch for dehydration
sections.text: Watch for signs of dehydration (loss of body fluids) in children who have norovirus illness. Children who are dehydrated may cry with few or no tears and be unusually sleepy or fussy.

sections.heading: Drink plenty of liquids
sections.text: If you have norovirus illness, you should drink plenty of liquids to replace fluid lost from vomiting and diarrhea. This will help prevent dehydration.

sections.heading: Drink plenty of liquids
sections.text: Sports drinks and other drinks without caffeine or alcohol can help with mild dehydration. However, these drinks may not replace important nutrients and minerals. Oral rehydration fluids that you can get over the counter are most helpful for mild dehydration.

sections.heading: Seek medical care for severe dehydration
sections.text: Dehydration can lead to serious problems. Severe dehydration may require hospitalization for treatment with fluids given through your vein (intravenous or IV fluids). If you think you or someone you are caring for is severely dehydrated, call your doctor.
